prompt: Two kinds of questions, same model, same confident tone in the answer either way:

options.label: Well-represented in training data
options.content: "What year did the Berlin Wall fall?" - this fact appears constantly, consistently, across huge amounts of training text. The most plausible continuation and the true answer are the same thing here, so the model's confident-sounding answer (1989) is also correct. This is the common case, and it's exactly why hallucination doesn't feel like a constant problem in everyday use.

options.label: Obscure or fabricated-sounding
options.content: "What's the ISBN of [a real but obscure self-published book], and who wrote the foreword?" - if this specific detail was barely or never represented in training data, the model still produces its most plausible-sounding guess, delivered with the exact same fluent, confident tone as the correct answer above. Nothing in how it's phrased signals "I'm actually guessing here" - that distinction was never part of the generation process to begin with.
